Lessons.Title: Vertex Form
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: recognize vertex form a(x−h)²+k and use it to identify the vertex, axis and maximum/minimum, comparing it to standard and factored representations. First-party Edulytiks adaptation of Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition U06:L15 teacher https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/6/15/preparation.html and student https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/students/1/6/15/index.html (CC BY 4.0). The source introduces vertex form because previous work found extrema using intercepts.

Original function f(x)=2(x−3)²+4 has vertex(3,4), axis x3, opens upward and has minimum4. Expanded form2(x²−6x+9)+4=2x²−12x+22 yields y-intercept f(0)=22; factored form over real numbers is not possible because this function has no real zeros (all outputs≥4). Do not invent x-intercepts.

At x1, f=2(−2)²+4=12; at x5, f=2(2)²+4=12, demonstrating symmetry about x3. The coefficient2 makes vertical changes twice as large as those of y=(x−3)²+4 for the same displacement. The vertex coordinates are (h,k) because the squared term is zero at x=h.

Student task: match three forms/graphs, find vertex and explain why no horizontal intercept exists for this example, compare f with an alternate negative-coefficient parabola and support conclusions with algebra. Teacher-scored rubric0–2 each for vertex and axis, expanded equivalence, full graph feature explanation and symmetric-point evidence.

KeyConcepts.Title: Vertex form
KeyConcepts.Definition: A quadratic can be written a(x−h)²+k with vertex(h,k).
KeyConcepts.Rule: Set x=h to remove square term.

KeyConcepts.Title: Minimum or maximum
KeyConcepts.Definition: Positive a opens up and yields minimum k; negative a opens down and yields maximum k.

KeyConcepts.Title: Symmetry
KeyConcepts.Definition: Inputs equidistant from h give same output.

WorkedExamples.Title: Read vertex
WorkedExamples.Question: Find vertex, axis and range of f=2(x−3)²+4.
WorkedExamples.Method: Interpret the original vertex-form expression and verify its equivalent standard-form algebra.

WorkedExamples.Title: Rewrite as standard form
WorkedExamples.Question: Expand f=2(x−3)²+4.
WorkedExamples.Method: Interpret the original vertex-form expression and verify its equivalent standard-form algebra.
WorkedExamples.Check: Both forms agree at vertex and intercept.

WorkedExamples.Title: Check equal-height points
WorkedExamples.Question: Find f1 and f5.
WorkedExamples.Method: Interpret the original vertex-form expression and verify its equivalent standard-form algebra.
WorkedExamples.Check: Equal absolute deviations give equal squares.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Reading vertex x-coordinate with wrong sign

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A positive minimum may be above zero.

SummaryPoints: Vertex form reveals extremum and symmetry directly.
The original quadratic has vertex(3,4), minimum4 and no real zeros.
